context_blurb:
Seawater, a bronze statue and the air you breathe are all solutions: mixtures so even that no separate bits can be seen, however close you look. Every solution has a solvent, the part that does the dissolving, and at least one solute, the part dissolved in it. How fast a solid dissolves, and how much of it can, are things you can test with a few beakers.

The solvent is the part a solution holds the most of, and a solute is spread evenly through it. A solution need not be a liquid. Bronze is mostly copper with a little tin, the two melted and cooled into one even solid. In bronze, copper is the solvent because there is more of it, and the tin is a solute dissolved in the copper. Tin does make bronze harder, but hardness never decides the solvent; only the amount does. Chemists call metal solutions like bronze and brass alloys.

Water earns the name universal solvent because it dissolves more substances than any other liquid. That is why rain, rivers and blood carry dissolved minerals and nutrients wherever they go. The oxygen end of a water molecule is slightly negative and the hydrogen end slightly positive, so water tugs on charged particles and pulls the sodium and chloride of salt apart. Still, water cannot dissolve everything: iodine dissolves so poorly in it that tincture of iodine, an antiseptic put on cuts, is made with alcohol.

Concentration is how much solute a given amount of solution holds. Seawater has about 35 grams of salt in every kilogram. At low tide a rock pool is cut off, and a hot sun evaporates water from it, but the salt stays behind. The same salt now sits in less water, so the concentration rises, and a sun-baked pool can reach 50 grams or more in a kilogram. Rain does the opposite: it dilutes the pool with fresh water, and the concentration falls.

How fast a solid dissolves can be tested with pairs of beakers, for water can only work on a solid where it touches it. Try halite, natural rock salt: one lump in a beaker, an equal mass of crushed grains in another. The grains are gone first, because crushing bares far more surface to the water, while most of the lump hides inside, away from it. Heat speeds dissolving too. Drop matching crystals of blue copper sulfate into cold water and into hot, and the hot one vanishes first. In hot water the particles move faster, strike the crystal more often and carry its particles off sooner. The crystal dissolves; it does not melt, for copper sulfate never melts at all.

The water right against a crystal of Epsom salt soon fills with dissolved salt and takes up more only slowly, so stirring speeds things up by sweeping that water away and bringing fresh water to the crystal. Stirring, crushing and waiting change only how fast a solid dissolves, never how much the water can hold. Keep stirring potassium nitrate, a white crystalline salt, into some water, and at last extra crystals lie undissolved on the bottom: the solution is saturated, holding all the solute it can at that temperature. Only warming the water makes room for more, since warmer water holds more of most solids. Water near boiling holds over seven times as much potassium nitrate as water at 20 degrees Celsius.

Gases go the other way. Heat helps dissolved gas escape, so warm water holds less gas than cold: fresh water at 20 degrees Celsius can hold about 9 milligrams of oxygen in a litre, but at 30 degrees only about 7.6. That is why hot, calm summers can leave pond fish short of oxygen. Pressure matters too: the harder a gas presses on a liquid, the more of it the liquid holds. At the bottling plant, carbon dioxide is forced into chilled water under pressure, and a tight cap keeps the pressure in. Twist the cap off, and the pressure falls to that of ordinary air, so less gas can stay dissolved, and the extra carbon dioxide streams up as bubbles. Those bubbles were dissolved in the water all along; no air has to get in to make them.
